summary: Segment Routing encodes paths as sequences of segments that routing protocols advertise. This document extends the BGP Link State (BGP-LS) address family so Segment Routing information can be carried through BGP.

plainLanguage.summary: Segment Routing information can be advertised within an IGP area, while a network controller may need a wider view. This RFC lets BGP-LS carry SR details about nodes, links, and prefixes between areas and across a trusted domain.

questions: how does bgp-ls carry segment routing information
why does segment routing need bgp-ls
subtitle: How BGP-LS carries Segment Routing information beyond an individual IGP area.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing information advertised by an IGP is limited to that IGP's area. A controller using only the IGP view may lack information needed to build paths across areas or autonomous systems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds BGP-LS Attribute TLVs for SR information about nodes, links, and prefixes. The TLVs carry information derived from IS-IS, OSPFv2, and OSPFv3 advertisements, without changing BGP-LS NLRI encoding.
tldr.outcome: A BGP-LS consumer can collect SR topology and SID information across a trusted SR domain. The unit metadata says RFC 9085 is updated by RFC 9356.

today: RFC 9085 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9356. It defines BGP-LS Attribute TLVs for Segment Routing information.

sections.title: Why Segment Routing Uses BGP-LS
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) represents a path as a sequence of segments, each of which can describe a topological or service instruction. IGP protocols advertise SR identifiers and related information within an IGP area.

Because that information is flooded only within an area, a controller may not see enough topology to construct paths across multiple areas or autonomous systems. BGP-LS already carries link-state information through BGP; this RFC adds SR details to that channel.
sections.plainLanguage: An IGP advertises SR information within its area, but a controller may need a broader view. BGP-LS can carry those details across the trusted SR domain.

sections.title: How BGP-LS Collects the Information
sections.content:
In the described deployment, BGP speakers in IGP areas send information to route reflectors. The reflectors can collect link-state data from multiple areas and from other autonomous systems through external BGP peers. A consumer, such as a controller, obtains the information from a BGP speaker.

BGP-LS identifies a node, link, or prefix in the NLRI and carries its properties in the BGP-LS Attribute. This RFC extends the attribute; it does not change the NLRI encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP speakers send area-level network details to route reflectors, which can provide a wider view to a controller. This RFC adds fields to the information attribute while leaving the existing NLRI format unchanged.

sections.title: Node Attributes
sections.content:
Node Attribute TLVs carry SR capabilities, supported algorithms, local label ranges, Mapping Server preference, and SID or label values. They belong with the Node NLRI for the IGP node that originated the corresponding information.

For example, SR Capabilities can advertise ranges in the node's Segment Routing Global Base. The SR Local Block TLV reports ranges reserved for local SIDs, which helps a consumer understand what local values are available.
sections.plainLanguage: A node's attributes describe its SR capabilities, supported algorithms, and label ranges. A controller can use this information when planning a path through the node.

sections.title: Link Attributes
sections.content:
Link Attribute TLVs describe an Adjacency SID, LAN adjacencies, and Layer 2 bundle-member links. An Adjacency SID identifies a path over a particular link, and its weight can be used for load balancing.

A LAN Adjacency SID lets a node advertise adjacencies to other nodes on a LAN in one Link NLRI. Bundle-member information identifies an individual member of a bundled link and may include link attributes as sub-TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: Link attributes describe the SR identifiers and properties associated with links between routers. They also let BGP-LS describe multiple LAN neighbors or a member link in a bundle.

sections.title: Prefix Attributes
sections.content:
Prefix Attribute TLVs carry a Prefix-SID, prefix flags, the source router identifier, an OSPF router identifier where applicable, and ranges of prefix-to-SID mappings. A Prefix-SID associates an identifier or label with a prefix.

A Range TLV describes a group of prefix-to-SID mappings. Its Prefix NLRI counts as a normal routing prefix only when an IGP metric TLV is also associated with it.
sections.plainLanguage: Prefix attributes tell a consumer which SR identifier is associated with a destination prefix. A range can describe mappings for several prefixes together.

sections.title: Code Points and Processing Errors
sections.content:
IANA registered the TLV code points in the BGP-LS registry. Syntactic checks for malformed attributes include the new TLVs; a syntax error causes the BGP-LS Attribute to be discarded and logged.

BGP does not check whether the TLV content is semantically correct or associated with the right NLRI type. The consumer is responsible for that check, and incorrect data can prevent a path computation application from using the intended SR information.
sections.plainLanguage: The new TLV numbers are registered so BGP-LS speakers can identify each field. BGP checks whether the fields are well formed, while the receiving application checks whether their meaning and placement make sense.

sections.title: Keeping SR Information Within Its Domain
sections.content:
These extensions do not change the BGP-LS security model described by RFC 7752. They carry SR information originated by IGPs, which are assumed to use the security and authentication mechanisms required by their specifications.

SR information is intended for consumers inside a trusted SR domain. The RFC recommends isolating BGP-LS peering sessions so topology information is not advertised to external peers outside that domain.
sections.plainLanguage: SR topology information is intended for trusted consumers within the SR domain. Operators should isolate BGP-LS sessions from external BGP sessions that do not need this information.
